title: High-Resolution Imaging and Spectroscopy in STEM Below 10 Kelvin
content: Exploring the emergent properties and phases of quantum materials [1] requires cooling of the sample to temperatures an order of magnitude lower than liquid N2. Additionally, recent experiments indicate that radiation damage in single particle biological structure determination is lowered when the sample temperature is below liquid N2 [2]. These two developments are driving strong interest in electron microscope sample stages and holders that can reach temperatures of 10 K and below. An ideal sample cooling system of this type should achieve stabilities (drift and shakes) comparable to room temperature sample holders and be compatible with a variety of sample holders. It should also pay close attention to cryoshielding, so that surfaces at room temperature close to the sample do not raise its temperature by thermal radiation, and to the sample stage vacuum system, so that ice contamination of the cooled sample is prevented.
